takeaway: Primary retroperitoneal sarcoma is managed by complete en bloc resection. Image-guided core biopsy is standard. After STRASS, routine neoadjuvant radiotherapy is not recommended [1].
clinicalQuestion: What is the standard operation and the role of preoperative radiotherapy?
background: Liposarcoma accounts for about half of retroperitoneal sarcomas. Leiomyosarcoma carries a higher risk of distant metastasis [1].
intervention: Percutaneous core biopsy and macroscopically complete en bloc resection.
comparator: Routine neoadjuvant radiotherapy, tested in STRASS.
primaryOutcome: Complete resection and avoidance of ineffective routine radiotherapy.
mainFindings: Complete en bloc gross resection is the cornerstone. Surgery should produce one specimen containing the tumour and involved contiguous organs. Image-guided coaxial core needle biopsy, 14–18 gauge, is strongly recommended. Biopsy may occasionally be omitted if an expert judges the imaging pathognomonic, for example heterogeneous dedifferentiated or well-differentiated liposarcoma. STRASS compared preoperative radiotherapy plus surgery with surgery alone. On the primary endpoint of abdominal recurrence-free survival, routine neoadjuvant radiotherapy is not recommended [1].
clinicalMeaning: Biopsy, then plan one en bloc specimen. Do not add preoperative radiotherapy as a routine [1].
limitations: The consensus grades individual statements. This summary uses the resection, biopsy, and STRASS conclusions that were read in full [1].
bottomLine: One complete specimen. Core biopsy unless imaging is pathognomonic. No routine neoadjuvant radiotherapy [1].
practiceImplication: Refer before an unplanned open biopsy or a piecemeal resection [1].
trustRationale: Updated specialist consensus citing a phase 3 radiotherapy trial.
whatNotToOverclaim: Do not say radiotherapy has no role in every subtype; the statement is against routine use.
